In this section we will look at tidymodels.Tidymodels represents a
complete suite of packages designed to simplify machine learning in R.
We will focus on the following core components:

- `rsample`: split datasets into test / training / validation. Also
  includes tools for cross validation

- `recipes`: define a series of steps to pre-process data `parsnip`:
  easy way to try out lots of different models

- `tune`: optimise model hyperparameters (also `dials` which helps with
  tuning)

- `workflows`: bring together sampling, recipes, models and tuning into
  a single workflow

- `yardstick`: check the performance of models `broom`: extract
  important information from models

- There are also various additional packages, more information can be
  found at <https://www.tidymodels.org/packages/>

The easiest way to load these packages is to just call:

```         
library(tidymodels)
```

## Our dataset

For this tutorial we'll be using the `BreastCancer` dataset from the
`mlbench` package. Let's load the `BreastCancer` dataset and take a
quick look:


::: {.cell exercise='ex_loaddata'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_loaddata
#| 
data(BreastCancer, package = 'mlbench')
glimpse(______)
```
:::


:::: {.hint exercise="ex_loaddata"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`glimpse` is a tool to preview a dataset. Use the name of the dataset
inside `glimpse()`
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="ex_loaddata"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution:

Use the `glimpse()` function from `dplyr`:

``` r
data(BreastCancer, package = 'mlbench')
glimpse(BreastCancer)
```

1.  Load the BreastCancer dataset from the `mlbench` package,
2.  Use `glimpse()` to preview the data.
:::
::::

It looks like we have:

- One ID column `Id`

- 9 predictors `Cl.thickness`, `Cell.size`, `Cell.shape`,
  `Marg.adhesion`, `Epith.c.size`, `Bare.nuclei`, `Bl.cromatin`
  `Normal.nucleoli`, `Mitoses`

- A dichotymous output variable `Class`

We can explore this by creating a data table stratified by `Class`. To
do this we'll use the `gtsummary` packge and the function
`tbl_summary()`

> We don't want `Id` included in our table, so we'll exclude it first
> using `dplyr`'s `select()` function. We then build the table.


::: {.cell exercise='ex_basicsummary'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_basicsummary
#| 
BreastCancer |>
	dplyr::select(-______) |>
	gtsummary::tbl_summary(by = 'Class')

```
:::


:::: {.hint exercise="ex_basicsummary"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`dplyr::select` allows us to remove fields from our dataset by
prepending a variable (e.g. `Id`) with a '-' sign
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="ex_basicsummary"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution:

``` r
BreastCancer |>  #<1>
    dplyr::select(-Id) |>. #<2>
    gtsummary::tbl_summary(by = 'Class'). #<3>
```

Use the `select()` function from `dplyr` 1. The symbol '\|\>' is a
pipe - it passed the output from one function and passes it straight
into the next. In the first line it simply passed the dataset
BreastCancer into the next function. 2. Removes -Id column then data
frame less the Id column is passed to the table builder function
`tbl_summary` from the `gtsummary` package 3. Builds our table with
separate columns for each class (benign/malignant)
:::
::::

### Data type conversion

Most of our predictors are factors, but we'll probably want to treat
these as continuous variables from now on.

If we want to consider our predictors as continuous variables, we'll
need to change their type first. To do this we need to first convert
them into character strings, then convert those into numbers. We can use
`dplyr`'s `mutate` function to do this:


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
BreastCancer_old <- BreastCancer # make a copy before we change things

BreastCancer <- BreastCancer |>
	dplyr::select(-Id) |>
	dplyr::mutate(across(-Class, function(x) {
		x |> as.character() |> as.numeric()
		})
		) 

glimpse(BreastCancer)
```
:::


This is a bit more complex than what we've done before. `mutate()`
creates or changes variables. across() applys our custom function to any
variables except 'Class'. Our custom function takes each column,
converts it to a character, then converts that to number. We need to do
it like this because R treats factors differently.

## Univariate analysis

> We can now rebuild the table and add the `add_p` function at the end
> to run a univariate analysis on our predictors


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
BreastCancer |>
	gtsummary::tbl_summary(by = 'Class', type = list(everything() ~ 'continuous')) |>
	gtsummary::add_p()

```
:::


These all look like really useful features for predicting cell
malignancy even in a univariate analysis. This isn't always the case,
and even if a predictor performs poorly in a univariate analysis, it may
still perform well in a multivariate analysis.

## Logistic regression model

We can go ahead and build a simple logistic regression model with all
these predictors.

We need to define a `formula` which takes looks something like this:
`response_variable ~ predictor_variables`

The `predictor_variables` could be a list (e.g.
`Cell.size + Cell.shape + Mitoses`), or we can use the wildcard `.` for
all variables except the reponse variable.

Exercise: 1. Build and run a logistic regression model. Set data to
`BreastCancer` and `family` to `'binomial'` 2. Call `summary()` on our
new model to get a summary of the model output


::: {.cell exercise='ex_basiclogistic'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_basiclogistic
#| 

library(stats) # Loads the stats package which contains the glm function

bc_model_logistic <- # where we will store our model
	glm(Class ~ .,   # our formula
			data = ______, 
			family = '______')

# Take a look at the model summary:
summary(______)
```
:::


:::: {.hint exercise="ex_basiclogistic"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

`data =` is our dataset `family` = should be binomial for logistic
regression
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="ex_basiclogistic"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution:

``` r
# where we will store our model
bc_model_logistic <- 
    glm(Class ~ .,   # our formula
            data = BreastCancer, 
            family = 'binomial')

# Take a look at the model summary:
summary(bc_model_logistic)
```
:::
::::

Another way to display the regression results is to use the
`tbl_regression()` from `gtsummary`. We'll add the `exponentiate = TRUE`
argument so we get odds ratios rather than log(odds) - this makes it
much easier to interpret:

The extra line `gtsummary::add_glance_source_note()` adds some model
performance details to the table caption. `bold_p` ... I'm sure you can
work out what that does.


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
bc_model_logistic <- 
    glm(Class ~ .,   # our formula
            data = BreastCancer, 
            family = 'binomial')

bc_model_logistic |>
	gtsummary::tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) |>
	gtsummary::add_glance_source_note() |>
	gtsummary::bold_p()
```
:::


### Plotting model effects

And we can use the `plot_model()` function from `sjPlot` to quickly
render a graph showing the effect sizes of each predictor:


::: {.cell exercise='ex_basicsjPlot'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_basicsjPlot
#| 
library(sjPlot)

model_effect_plot <- bc_model_logistic |>
	sjPlot::plot_model()
	
______

```
:::


:::: {.hint exercise="ex_basicsjPlot"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint 1

Just call the name of your plot object to display it
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="ex_basicsjPlot"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Fully worked solution:

``` r
library(sjPlot)

model_effect_plot <- bc_model_logistic |>
    sjPlot::plot_model()
    
model_effect_plot
```
:::
::::

Nice! That was pretty easy, wasn't it?

Our `model_effect_plot` is a ggplot object, which means we can modify
it, e.g.


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
# Change the theme and title
model_effect_plot +
	ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
	ggplot2::ggtitle('Breast cancer predictors', subtitle = 'Logistic regression model')
```
:::


### Visualising our model

Wouldn't it be great if we could make some graphs which show predicted
outcomes for different combinations of predictors?

It looks like `Cl.thickness`, `Bl.cromatin` and `Bare.nuclei` are pretty
good predictors. We can use sJPlot again, but this time in `'pred'`
mode, which plots predictions.


::: {.cell}
```{webr}
library(sjPlot)

sjPlot::plot_model(bc_model_logistic, 
			 type = 'pred',
			 terms = c("Cl.thickness", "Bare.nuclei", "Bl.cromatin[0,5,10]"))
```
:::


So predictions are 0-100%. As malignancy is a binary output, we need to
set a threshold to make a hard call between benign vs malignant. Where
we set that will affect how sensitive and how precise our models are.
This is the basis of the ROC curve and tells us how good our models are.

A few important things to note about our model:

1.  Some predictors don't seem to be very good.

2.  It assumes that all predictors have a linear response. If we look at
    the categorical data before we converted it to numbers, we can see
    that sometimes the responses rise, peak and then fall again. Our
    logistic regression model misses this.

3.  Some variables correlate with each other. In a logistic regression,
    the effect is split across those variables and is diluted. We could
    be missing something important!

4.  If we look at our model output we see:

    `(16 observations deleted due to missingness)`

If any subject has any missing data, they get dropped from the analysis
completely.

We will now look at how we can deal with 1, 2, 3 and 4.

1.  We could simplify our model by removing ineffective predictors -
    there is a fine balance between gaining information from extra
    predictors and overfitting (model too complex). Removing predictors
    can effect the model, especially if there are cryptic associations
    with other variables. We'll look at ways to optimise models later.
2.  We could transform the data which shows a non-linear response.
3.  We could remove correlated variables, keeping the ones with most
    information
4.  Missing data can be a) ignored, and accept that we lose some
    data; b) treated by removing predictors with high levels of
    missingness; c) interpolated (e.g. replacing missings with mean
    values).

In the next stages we will look at feature selection, and model
optimisation.
